A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cultural-alignment study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions, relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments with five LLMs using WVS and Hofstede questions across Germany, Bangladesh and the USA, including results in Tables 1–3 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds Philippines results, thematic WVS analyses and an independent annotation-agreement check.

M1.justification: The four probing procedures, anthropological prompting and GPT-4o mapping of free-form responses remain unchanged. Appendix prompts receive small wording corrections; the additional Claude check validates the existing procedure.

E1.justification: v3 extends the existing WVS and Hofstede evaluations to the Philippines, including Filipino prompts. This is a targeted addition to the retained three-country coverage; the thematic analyses reuse the existing WVS questions.

E2.justification: Section 3.2 adds Claude Sonnet 3.7 as an independent comparison annotator against GPT-4o on 100 responses. The five original LLMs and four probing approaches remain in the main cultural-alignment comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds a separate 100-response cross-annotator validation and four-model Philippines comparisons. The established experiments retain their model versions, temperature 0.7, top-p 1 and core alignment metrics; newly documented blinding does not establish that the earlier review procedure changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing refusal and option-order analyses, v3 adds cross-annotator validation, human–LLM disagreement analysis in Section 5, and seven-theme WVS breakdowns in Appendix D.3. Philippines experiments also investigate the cultural-refusal and language-resource hypotheses.

E5.justification: v3 adds Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting across models in Figure 9. Existing significance tests and Hofstede quartile plots remain; the additions do not document new random seeds or repeated runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and v1 Table 11/v3 Table 12 retain their numerical results, while v3 adds thematic WVS scores, Philippines results, annotation agreement and revised Figure 3 projections. For example, Table 4 reports DeepSeek-R1 fully unconstrained correlations of 0.83 in both English and Filipino. Some new Figure 9 aggregates disagree with the retained Table 1 scores.

T1.justification: The hard and soft alignment definitions and Hofstede equations remain unchanged. The new statistical checks and conceptual criticisms introduce no formal theoretical results or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the claims that response constraints and option ordering affect measured alignment, and that evaluation should use flexible approaches focused on cultural proxies. Reorganizing the contribution list does not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v3 broadens the Bengali resource-scarcity explanation to cross-language biases after considering Filipino and German results. It also discusses annotation ambiguity and limited statistical significance, adds study-specific limitations, and introduces survey-validity and temporal-comparability concerns in Appendix A.3.

D1.justification: Sections 3.2 and 5 newly document Python remapping of reversed answers and independent, blinded human annotation with consensus resolution. The main prompts, model versions and decoding settings were already provided in v1.

R1.justification: The literature discussion adds multilingual-versus-cultural alignment work by Rystrøm et al., extrinsic evaluation by Bhatt and Diaz, and cultural-identity benchmarks by Das et al. New Appendix A.3 substantially broadens the conceptual grounding through prior criticisms of survey construct validity, cross-survey comparability and static national culture scores.

P1.justification: v3 refines terminology and wording, reorganizes the contribution list, inserts annotation and limitations sections, swaps Appendices B and C, and moves former Appendix F into E.6. Much of the existing prose and overall narrative sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from five radar charts to four annotated heatmaps. Figure 3 replaces the two-model Germany display with Llama 3.3 projections across three countries, while new Table 4 and Figures 7–9 add Philippines and thematic displays; retained appendix material is also relocated.

improvement.justification: The independent annotation check, disagreement analysis and expanded limitations improve validation and interpretation. However, new Figure 9 reports 65% mean Bangladesh English reverse-order hard alignment, although every corresponding score in the retained Table 1 is between 40% and 60%. The PDF provides no explanation for this discrepancy, leaving the reliability of the added quantitative evidence and the net quality improvement uncertain.
